NereusSDR on iPhone and iPad

The workspace look, every other screen

The phone screens from the design board, recoloured with the desktop 2026.10.1 workspace palette. Spectrum, waterfall, band plan, slice colours and frequency readouts are unchanged.

Look Today (navy) Workspace Press T or W to flip. The page keeps its place.

NEW FOR REVIEW · Choose the meters over the waterfall

Your direction: blend the tabs with tap-to-change gauges. The proposed blend is first, with the earlier comparison preserved below. Tabs choose a meter set; tapping a gauge changes that slot in the selected tab. Each tab keeps its own choices. Amp and Tuner appear only when configured; a configured accessory stays visible but disabled while offline. All names and readings are examples. PTT starts and stops each phone; choosing meters only changes the display.

The blend: tabs and tappable gauges

Tabs with tap-to-change meters

Tap Radio, Amp, Tuner or Custom to switch sets. Tap any gauge to replace just that slot. The meter source stays named.

Change an amplifier meter

Amp starts with output, SWR and temperature. Here its third gauge is changed to ALC Gain. Radio, Tuner and Custom keep their own choices.

The same blend in the picker and without equipment

Pick a reading for this tab

The picker changes one gauge in the selected tab. Choosing a reading keeps you on that tab; Done closes without a change.

Radio and Custom without equipment

Only Radio and Custom appear. Equipment meters are omitted from the picker too. You can still customize either tab; PTT stays clear.

Configured equipment and a temporary disconnect

Amplifier only

An amplifier is configured, with no tuner. Radio, Amp and Custom fill the tab row; tuner meters are omitted from the picker.

Configured amplifier offline

Amp stays visible but disabled with an offline reason. Its saved choices remain for reconnection. The tuner is still available.

The blend with larger text

Larger text on Pro Max

Tabs stay finger-sized and every gauge is tappable. Mic, EQ and ALC are the starting Custom set, with the other stage readings available in the picker.

The two earlier options

Swipe between meter pages

Radio, Amp, Tuner and Custom are visible buttons. Swipe across the gauges to move between pages. Custom chooses three readings before or during an over.

Tap a meter to replace it

Each gauge has a small arrow and a finger-sized tap target. Tap one to choose its source. Mix radio, amplifier, tuner and audio readings.

What you can put in the same overlay

Amplifier page

Power Genius XL output and SWR with its temperature below. The source is named so its readings are distinct from the radio.

Tuner page

Tuner Genius XL power and SWR with Mic level below. Switching meters does not start the tuner.

Mic, EQ and ALC

A custom mixture of Mic level, EQ and ALC Gain. The other ALC and processing-stage readings are also choices.

Today and the meter picker

Current overlay

The existing RF power, SWR and Mic level gauges, with no new meter controls. The surrounding phone is the same in every example.

Choose a replacement

The picker names each meter and its equipment. A choice replaces only the gauge you tapped. Done closes without a change.

Unavailable equipment and larger text

No amplifier or tuner

Only Radio and Custom appear when neither accessory is configured. Their meters are omitted from the picker; available readings still work.

Larger text on Pro Max

The same page controls and gauge choices on the larger phone. Text and meter targets grow while the flag keeps the existing board layout.

NEW FOR REVIEW · Diversity on any slice, with a DIV badge

Diversity is no longer tied to slice A. The radio has one Diversity, so one slice uses it at a time. You turn it on from that slice's flag, as you would NR, and the flag shows a small DIV badge on every device. Turning it on for another slice moves it there with a short note. Each slice keeps its own phase and gain, so moving back brings them back. The Diversity page shows the slice using it, with one button to bring it to the slice you are using. Every button and slider here is live: tap it. Slices, frequencies, phases, gains and device names are example data. NereusSDR keeps one dark look, so the light and dark frames match.

The flag: the DIV badge, and turning it on

Slice B uses Diversity, so its flag carries the green DIV badge, under the filter width next to TX, so TX keeps its full size. Slice A's flag has no badge. The More menu of a slice has a switch for Diversity on that slice; when another slice has it, the line under the switch says the switch moves it. The last row shows the move on a radio with older firmware: it works the same.

The button greyed, with the reason.

One Diversity, on any slice. The radio has one Diversity. The slice using it shows a green DIV badge on its flag, on the phone, the iPad and the desktop. You turn it on from a slice's flag, in its More menu on the phone or its right-click menu on the desktop.

Moving it. Turning it on for another slice moves it there at once, with a short note such as "Diversity moved from B to C. Both slices paused briefly." There is no need to turn it off first, and the sound on both slices stops for a moment while it moves. Each slice keeps its own phase and gain, so moving it back brings them back.

The page and the dialog. Both show the slice using Diversity. When you are using another slice, one button brings it to yours. When it is off, the same button starts it on your slice.

When it cannot change. Changing or moving it needs control of the slice using it; when another device has that slice, its settings show greyed with who controls it. A radio with one antenna input, such as the Hermes Lite 2, shows Diversity greyed with that reason, and so does a radio with no receiver channel to spare. While the radio transmits with PureSignal, Diversity pauses, greyed, where PureSignal borrows its receiver channels; on older firmware it keeps running. Older firmware works the same way; when every receiver is in use, the button to move it is greyed with that reason.

Turned sideways, and the iPad

Sideways, the chip keeps to the top of the band, inside the safe area and left of the dBm scale. The band is too short for the chip to fit under a flag, so it moves left of the flag instead. On the iPad it sits at the top right of the band, beside the applet column.

Sideways, the flag in the top right

Slice A near the top of the band: its flag fills the spectrum's height, so the chip sits to the left of the flag and its buttons.

iPad, WIDE

The chip at the top right of the band, left of the dBm scale.

What it shows. The amber WIDE chip is the desktop's WIDE mark: the radio's receive filters are bypassed for the first receiver input, so that input is not Filtered.

When it appears. Only while that input is not Filtered. When the input is Filtered again, the chip goes away. It sits at the top right of the band, left of the dBm scale. When a flag, the Back to your band bar or a slice marker is there, the chip moves down below it, and to the left if the frequency scale is in the way. It never covers any of them.

What a tap does. It opens the flag's More menu under the chip, with the reasons already there under Filter policy: whether the input is filtered, the Core's reason, and, when one slice sets a filter for the whole input, which slice and why. A tap anywhere else closes it. The chip's target is at least 44 pt each way, and nothing else opens it.

NEW FOR REVIEW · Receive level calibration and the preamp list

The Core now runs Thetis's receive level calibration and a ten-entry preamp list, with a preamp of its own for the second receiver input. The desktop and the phone both ask the Core; neither runs it. On the phone, Level Cal sits where the desktop has it, Setup → Hardware → Hardware Config → Calibration, with the desktop's fields, buttons, progress bar and status line in its words. The preamp list stays in the Modes tab's Front end, with the labels the Core sends for the connected radio. Every change uses a visible, labelled button; nothing needs a press and hold, a swipe or a hidden gesture, and the run never keys the radio. Radios, frequencies, levels, percentages and device names are example data.

AbcDotted underline: the phone's own words, for your call. Neither the Core nor the desktop has words here. The underline is a board marking, not part of the screen.

Dashed amber ring: arrives with a Core update. The Core knows the second receiver input's own preamp list but does not send it to the phone today; the phone draws it now for your approval. The ring is a board marking, not part of the screen.

The preamp list

Modes → Front end, Preamp:, for the slice picked at the top. A slice on the first receiver input shows the catalog's list for the connected radio; a slice on the second shows that input's own list. On a radio with one receiver input every slice shows the one list.

While a run holds the receiver

The Core sets the calibrated slice for the run and puts it all back at the end: RIT off, AM, the calibration frequency, the attenuators off and the preamps at 0dB. Each device shows those as it shows any change. PTT stays live, since the Core does not lock it; keying stops the run, and the Calibration page says why. Nothing else on the band changes. Slice B stays where it was, off this part of the band.

NEW FOR REVIEW · Taking control of a slice

Your ruling: taking a slice keeps it exactly as it is, with every setting kept, and the device that had it is told and can take it back. While this phone listens to a slice another device controls, that slice's flag says who controls it and carries a labelled Take control button. Its frequency, mode and filter show as usual; the controls that would change it are dimmed until this phone controls it. The slice's sound keeps playing here throughout. Every word on the phones below is the Core's own, except where a card says otherwise. Device names (Shack desktop, Shack phone, Garden phone), frequencies and times are example data.

A slice another device controls

Listening to slice B

Slice B belongs to Shack desktop and this phone listens to it. The flag names the device and has Take control, a plain button: no press and hold, swipe or hidden tap. Tap it here to see what follows.

A slice nobody controls

Slice C is open on the Core with no device controlling it, for example after its device disconnected. The same flag and the same button.

Large type

At a large text size the words and the button grow and wrap; the flag grows taller, never wider, and the button stays a full row.

After taking it

Nothing about the slice changes: the Core moves only who controls it. The same frequency, mode and filter, before and after. Example: slice B on 7.249.000 LSB, 2.9 kHz.

Controlled here

The owner line and the button go; the flag's controls light up. Shack desktop keeps listening to slice B.

The first key after taking it

Transmit stays where it was (slice A here). The first press of PTT after a take-over does not key; the Core says to choose the slice for transmit with its TX button, ringed here.

The first key, large type

The notice wraps over more lines at a large text size.

On the device that had it

A second phone, Garden phone, had slice B; Shack phone took it. Garden phone is told who took it and keeps listening, and its flag now says who controls slice B. A device that was away is told when it comes back.

Dashed amber ring: arrives with a Core update. The Core is adding one-tap Take back on this notice. The phone draws the button now so you can approve its final look. The ring is a board marking, not part of the screen.

Told, still listening

The notice with Take back. Take back asks the Core the same way Take control does. Tap it here to see it come back.

Told, large type

The notice and its button wrap; Take back keeps a full-size target.

    NEW FOR REVIEW · RADE on the VFO flag

    While a slice is in RADE (RADE-U or RADE-L), its flag gains the desktop's RADE row under the S-meter: who is talking, whether the Core is locked on to the signal, and the signal-to-noise ratio in real time, with the frequency offset after it. The row holds the word RADE until the other station's end-of-over frame brings its callsign; then the callsign takes RADE's place. The mode tab turns purple and reads RADE-U or RADE-L, as on the desktop. In any other mode the row is not there at all. The row only shows readings; it adds no buttons and nothing to press, and tapping the flag still makes its slice active. Callsigns, readings and frequencies here are example data (K1ABC and W1XYZ stand in for real stations). The SNR moves on its own in the live pictures; the band is drawn by the board.

    On the flag

    Receiving, callsign known

    The Core is locked on (filled dot) and has decoded the callsign from the last end of over. SNR 5 dB or more is green. Example: K1ABC, 12 dB, 38 Hz off.

    Receiving, no callsign

    Locked on in the middle of an over. The callsign only comes at the over's end, so the row says RADE until then. Example readings.

    A weak signal

    Under 5 dB the dot turns yellow, the desktop's sign of marginal copy. Example: 3 dB.

    No signal, not locked on

    Nothing to decode in the passband: a hollow grey dot and "---" for the SNR. This is also how the row starts when a slice enters RADE.

    An older Core

    A Core that does not send whether it is locked on. The row stays, greyed, and gives the reason in place of the readings. The mode tab still reads RADE-L.

    In LSB: no RADE row

    For contrast. The same slice in LSB: the flag ends at the mode tabs, exactly as it does now.

    Two slices: A in RADE, B in LSB

    Each flag follows its own slice's mode. A shows the row; B, in LSB, does not. Drawn with B's flag open below A's so both can be seen.

    Large type

    At a large text size the RADE row grows and wraps: the callsign on one line, the dot, SNR and offset on the next. The flag grows taller, never wider.

    When the callsign comes and goes

    The desktop's rules, which the Core applies, so the phone shows the same thing at the same moment. One example QSO with K1ABC, then W1XYZ, read left to right. Times are examples.

      NEW FOR REVIEW · The 3D spectrum view

      The desktop's 3D view on the phone: the spectrum above the frequency scale becomes a stack of the last 96 traces, the newest across the front and older ones leaning back and narrowing into the distance. Only the spectrum changes. The waterfall, the frequency scale, the band plan, the slice flags and every marker stay flat and where they are in 2D, so tuning works exactly as it does now. The switch is in the Display sheet, beside the phone's other display choices, and the same seven rows are in Setup, Display, 3D View. Each pan keeps its own 3D settings on this phone, except 3D Floor, which each band keeps. Signals, levels and the Core are example data, and the 3D pictures are drawn by the board, not by the app. Tap 2D and 3D, move the sliders and try Reset in the sheets; tap or drag the band to tune.

      The switch, in Display

      NEW FOR REVIEW · Settings backup and restore

      Setup → Diagnostics → Export / Import, where the desktop has it. Back up saves the Core’s settings and this phone’s settings in one file, NereusSDR.nereus-settings, the same kind of file a NereusSDR remote window on a computer saves, and hands it to the Share sheet. No pairing key is ever in it. Restore opens that file from the app, from Files or from the Share sheet, shows what it holds, names the other devices connected to the Core and asks before anything changes; then the Core applies its part with a radio reconnect, the other devices reconnect by themselves, and this phone applies its own part. Every change uses a visible, labelled button; nothing needs a press and hold, a swipe or a hidden gesture, and nothing here keys the radio. The Core, device names, file names, sizes and times are example data. The Core’s refusal words for a restore are examples too: today’s Core can back up but cannot restore, and its restore note will give the real ones. Apple’s Share sheet and file picker are drawn generic.

      Back up

      Where it is

      Setup → Diagnostics, the fifth row, marked Both because it holds the Core’s settings and this phone’s.

      Export / Import

      What a backup holds, each part tagged Core or This phone, and a line of its own saying no pairing key is included. Example Core.

      Getting the Core’s part

      Progress while the Core’s settings come over the link, then each later step. Cancel is a labelled button; leaving the page cancels too. Example sizes.

      The Share sheet

      Only once every part is checked does the one file go to Apple’s Share sheet, drawn generic. You choose where it goes.

      Backed up

      A line under the button says when and where. Example time and place.

      The Core refuses: on the air

      The Core’s words, as it sends them, and that nothing was saved. Back up stays ready for another try.

      A backup that fails

      The link changed part way, or a length, checksum or contents check failed: nothing is saved, never a part of a file. The desktop’s own words.

      Today’s Core

      It can send its settings, so Back up works. It cannot restore a backup, so Open a backup is greyed with the reason.

      An older Core

      It cannot send its settings: Back up is greyed with the reason, and so is Open a backup.

      Open a backup from the app

      Or from Files or the Share sheet

      In Files, Mail or Messages, Share and then NereusSDR opens the Restore page with that file. Drawn generic; example files.

      What the file holds

      The file is checked whole before anything else. Then its two parts, that it holds no pairing keys, and what will happen. Example file.

      A file opened on today’s Core

      The question

      The question, no other device

      The Core applies its part

      The Core’s settings go to the Core, it applies them and reconnects the radio. The band pauses meanwhile. Example sizes.

      The other devices reconnect

      The radio is back. Each other device reconnects by itself, and the page shows each one as it does. Example devices.

      Restored, with this phone’s part

      This phone applies its own part last and says what changed; pairing is unchanged. Example time.

      Not a NereusSDR backup

      Connection at a glance

      One slim 24-point information row below the toolbar and above the slice labels. It shows network, active path and measured app traffic. Native app changes follow review of this board.

      APPROVED LAYOUT · Connection and performance

      Tools → Connection and performance. These are labelled example fixtures, not live readings or an implemented phone feature. The selector changes one destination between Connection, Round trip, Audio, Core, and Details. Scroll inside each phone; chart Help and series controls are visible.

      Moving the split, and the dBm scale's arrows

      New, drawn again for your approval: nothing is added to the band's height. The split starts at the desktop's 40% spectrum and 60% waterfall; the frequency scale between them is the handle, marked by a small ≡ at its left end, and Display gets a Spectrum height slider. The dBm scale gets the desktop's two arrows.

      On the band

      40% spectrum and 60% waterfall. Drag the frequency scale up or down to move the split. The dBm scale has ▲ at its top and ▼ at its bottom.

      The Display sheet

      One new row, Spectrum height, after Line and before Top: 20% to 80%, starting at 40%. The band plan rows have moved to Setup.

      • The split starts at the desktop's 40% spectrum.
      • Drag the frequency scale, or set Spectrum height in Display. Kept per pan on this phone.

      Tuning on the band

      New, for your approval, from your first test on the Pi: a drag on the band moves the band, a drag on a flag or its passband tunes that slice, each slice has a tuning step you can pick, and a tap on the flag's frequency lets you type one. All four use what the Core already sends: the slice's step and the radio's list of steps.

      Drag the band

      The band slides left and right, as on the desktop. Slice A stays where it is; its flag moves with the band and comes back into view when the band does.

      Drag a flag or its passband

      Slice A tunes, in its step, while your finger moves. A tap on empty band still tunes there at once.

      The tuning step

      The step sits on the flag. A tap lists the radio's steps; the one you pick is slice A's, used by drags, taps (when snap is on) and the dial.

      Type a frequency

      A tap on the flag's frequency opens a number pad. Type it in MHz or kHz; Enter tunes slice A there.

      The Pan and Display buttons

      New, for your approval: the toolbar's Pan 1 and Display had nothing to open. Pan 1 takes the desktop's pan-level controls (its BAND grid, +RX, +TNF, the extended view); Display takes the pan's display settings, which are this phone's own.

      Pan 1

      The band grid (a band opens where the slice last was on it), a slice or a notch added here, and the extended view.

      Display

      This pan's look on this phone: the waterfall's palette and levels, the fill, the scale, and the Core's extras on the band.

      Several devices: states and notices

      What the screens in the next section don't show: the messages that appear over the band when something happens involving another device, and the states in between (a device that's away, transmit on its way, a slice held by the radio's mic). The same cast as the next section: this phone has slice A on 40 m, the MacBook has slices B and D and has transmit, the iPad has slice C on 20 m.

      Notices

      Back, without transmit

      The phone’s link dropped and it came back within 3 minutes. It didn’t have transmit, so there’s nothing about transmit to say.

      Back, transmit taken meanwhile

      It had transmit, and the MacBook took it while the phone was away. The phone doesn’t get it back by itself; Take it back asks first.

      Back after 3 minutes

      Away longer than 3 minutes: the Core saved its slices and brings them back, but transmit went free, so PTT reads Tap for whoever presses first.

      Back after 3 minutes, Core full

      Away longer than 3 minutes while four other devices filled the Core: the phone gets the fifth-device question, saying why.

      A slice that couldn’t come back

      Coming back, one of the phone’s slices finds every receiver taken. Its frequency and settings wait on the Core.

      The antenna stays

      Your call: tuning across a band edge doesn’t switch the antenna while another device listens through it, and the phone says so.

      The Core is busy

      The same chip as when the connection is full, when it’s the Core’s processing that runs short instead.

      Short, nobody has transmit

      With nobody holding transmit (or the radio’s mic holding it), no device keeps a full share, so the note says they share.

      The states in between

      A device that's away

      The MacBook's link dropped while it had transmit. The Core keeps transmit for it, unkeyed, for up to 3 minutes. Its label greys with "away", and taking transmit asks without the red button, since nobody is on the air.

      Transmit on its way

      Right after Unkey and take over, the Core unkeys the MacBook, then hands transmit over. For that moment PTT waits with a turning ring; once it reads Tap, one tap keys.

      Held by the radio's mic

      On a Core with no desktop, the radio's own mic keys on the transmit slice, here this phone's slice A. The flag says ON AIR, the frequency greys, and tuning slice A waits until the press ends.

      Away, on Devices

      Setup, Devices marks a device whose link dropped as away, with how long. It keeps its place and its slices for 3 minutes.

      Away, for a fifth device

      A device that's away has been idle longest, so a fifth device's list starts on it.

      Several devices at once

      Your calls: up to four devices on one Core at the same time, each with its own slices and pans, and one of them holding transmit. Other devices’ slices show on your band, labelled and out of reach. Anything that would disturb another device asks first and names it, and that device is told, with Take it back. This replaces the takeover question: a second device now simply connects, and taking a place only comes up for a fifth. On every screen here this phone has slice A on 40 m, the MacBook at the shack has slices B (sharing this phone’s receiver) and D and has transmit, and the iPad has slice C on 20 m.

      Slices and transmit

      Another device’s slice

      The MacBook’s slice B on your band: a dashed line in B’s colour and a label with the device’s name, but no flag, so there’s nothing to drag. The label opens a note saying whose it is. TX on the label and the MacBook on your PTT button both say it has transmit.

      Taking transmit

      Tap PTT while another device has transmit, and it asks first. Whoever has transmit is the control operator. Take transmit, then tap PTT again to go on the air.

      While it’s on the air

      Your call: the band shows the MacBook’s transmission, PTT turns red with its name, and the button says Unkey and take over. The Core unkeys the MacBook before transmit moves.

      Transmit taken from you

      The device that had transmit is told who took it and when. Take it back asks the same question the other way.

      Taken at the radio

      Your call: pressing the radio’s own PTT, its mic or a footswitch, takes transmit with no question, because the press is the answer. Programs never take transmit this way; they transmit only while their own device has it. PTT names the radio until you take it back.

      When the Core runs short

      Your call: the device with transmit keeps its full band and sound, and the others slow down first. The chip stays while it lasts, like the one on cellular.

      Receivers and shared settings

      Every receiver in use

      A new slice that fits no receiver’s window, with none free, means taking one. It lists who has each receiver and what they’re doing, and you pick.

      Your receiver taken

      The other side: this phone’s slice closed, and it says who took the receiver and when. The connection stays up, and Take it back asks first.

      Moving a shared receiver

      Your call: you and the MacBook share a receiver, so going to 20 m asks first. With a receiver free, it would say slice B moves there instead of closing.

      Shared settings

      Your call: any device can change what every device hears, like the attenuator here, but it asks first when another device’s slices would feel it, and names them.

      Told afterwards

      The device that didn’t ask gets a note saying who changed what. Nothing to answer.

      Who’s connected

      Setup, Devices splits the devices connected now from the ones only paired, with each one’s slices and bands, and TX on the one with transmit.

      More than four

      A fifth device

      Your call: a fifth device picks one of the four to take the place of. It starts on the one idle longest. Picking the one on the air turns the button red, and the Core unkeys it first.

      Your own session

      After a lost link, the phone takes its own session back without asking: its slices, and transmit if no one took it meanwhile. You’re never locked out of your transmitter.

      On the device whose place was taken

      The iPad is told who took its place and when. Its band stops, its slices and settings stay on the Core, and Take it back asks the fifth-device question the other way.

      Transmit time-out

      Your call: from a phone or iPad, the station ends any transmission that runs past the time-out, three minutes to start with, which is Thetis's own default. The PTT is a toggle, so a missed second tap or a headset button pressed in a pocket would otherwise keep the radio on the air while the link is working fine. The desktop at the station keeps Thetis's time-out switched off.

      Setting it

      On the PTT buttons page, as a station setting: from thirty seconds to thirty minutes, or off. Tap the value to step through a few.

      When it fires

      The station unkeys and the band says why. PTT is back to Tap, and one tap starts a fresh transmission.

      New: long sessions

      Hours of listening, on a stand or in a pocket. Locked, the phone asks the station for sound only, which saves most of the battery and data; the lock-screen card still gets its readings. iOS ends the card after eight hours, so the app leaves a useful last message on it.

      Battery and sessions

      Sound only while locked; your call: the screen always stays on while the band is showing; a sleep timer; and slowing the band in Low Power Mode or when the phone runs hot.

      Back after a while locked

      The band picks up where it is now, and the waterfall marks the stretch that was sound only, so nothing looks missing by mistake.

      Eight hours in

      Just before iOS ends the card, the app gives it a last message. The sound carries on; opening NereusSDR starts a fresh card.

      A hardware PTT button

      iOS won't let an app turn the microphone on while the phone is locked, except through Apple's own Push to Talk system. It recognises a button on a headset, and the Action button can run a "begin or end transmission" action. So a button can key a phone in your pocket, but only through Apple's system, and that bends your rule that a locked phone never transmits.

      PTT buttons

      The headset button, a paired Bluetooth PTT button and the Action button, all toggles like the PTT on the band. Whether they work with the phone locked is one switch.

      Keyed from your pocket

      Your call: a headset press keys the locked phone, through Apple's Push to Talk. The card turns red and Apple's blue pill and panel show. Another press unkeys; the card's UNKEY still waits for Face ID.

      On the band

      The PTT on screen follows the button, and says what keyed it.

      Audio and data use

      The station sends the band's sound as Opus at 24 kbit/s, the R3 plan's default, and the phone chooses how many frames a second of the band it asks for, which is most of the data. Data figures are estimates from the remote design's reference measurements until the bench measures ours.

      Audio on this phone

      Where the band plays and which microphone you talk into. The iPhone's own microphone keeps AirPods at full quality; theirs would drop both ways to phone-call quality.

      From the band

      Press and hold the speaker button to move the sound, without leaving the band.

      Headphones disconnected

      Your call (D68): when headphones or AirPods go away, the sound pauses and the band keeps showing. It plays on the speaker only after a tap.

      Data use

      One choice for Wi-Fi and one for cellular, with the cost of each per hour, a monthly counter and a warning.

      On cellular

      Your call: cellular starts at Balanced. The first time, the phone says so and what it costs; the chip stays while you're off Wi-Fi.

      FreeDV Reporter

      The desktop's FreeDV Reporter window, fitted to a phone: the same 14 columns folded into two lines per station, the same transmit, receive and message tints fading after six seconds, the band filter, QSY, lookups and your status message. The reporter connection runs at the station, so your station stays listed while the phone is away.

      Stations on the air

      Rust while a station transmits, slate while it's hearing someone, mauve when its message changes. Your call: a tap tunes there, as a double-click does on the desktop.

      Press and hold a station

      Every column for that station, with the desktop's right-click actions: tune, ask to QSY, look up, copy the callsign.

      Ask to QSY

      Pick the frequency (your slice, theirs, or one you type), then Send QSY. As on the desktop, your radio tunes there too.

      FreeDV in Spot Hub

      The desktop's FreeDV tab: the connection and hide-my-station at the station; miles and kHz on each phone.

      iPad held upright

      Held upright, the iPad is 834 points wide and 1,210 tall, with the same toolbar, flags, toggle PTT and tabs as on its side.

      Applets below the band

      Your call: the band keeps the full width, so both flags stay full, and the S-meter, RX and TX applets sit below it in three columns, like a radio's front panel. Turned on its side, the applets go back to the column on the right.

      The station's side

      The station is NereusSDR's daemon, running beside the radio. The remote design gives it three places to show its pairing code: on a computer, a Setup page; on a small box, a status page any browser on its own network can open while it is unclaimed, and nereusd pairing show over SSH. The code never goes to its log. Only the console or an already-paired device can reopen pairing.

      On a computer: waiting

      Your call: a switch in the desktop app, on a new Remote Access page under CAT & Network. The station keeps running after the app closes, so the phone can still reach the radio. Until a device pairs, the code shows here.

      On a computer: adding a device

      Once claimed, the page lists paired devices with Revoke, and Add a device shows a one-time code, the same one the phone's Devices page makes.

      On a small box: its status page

      Any browser on the network can open it. It only shows: nothing can be changed from it, so a neighbour on the Wi-Fi can't reopen pairing.

      On a small box: its console

      Over SSH, nereusd pairing show gives the code and nereusd status the state. The log never carries the code.

      Signal History on the Multimeter page · For review

      Proposed app screen: Setup > Display > Multimeter. The graph sits directly below the existing History duration integer control. The value, millisecond unit, minus/plus buttons and typed-value entry stay as in the app. The page retains its existing Both tag. This board uses an editable integer field as the working equivalent of the app's tappable value and number pad; both phone previews share their example settings. Display units and decimal settings affect meter readouts; the proposed history graph keeps its explicit dBm scale.

      Interactive board proposal. All controls below operate on example settings only; this is not a built app or live signal. All values and traces below are examples. The proposed graph follows the selected slice's Core peak signal in dBm. It collects only while this page is open and clears when you leave, change slice or change Core. Time runs from 60 seconds ago to Now, with gaps during transmit or unavailable readings. Change History duration with minus/plus or type an integer in its value field to redraw the time window; the default stays 60000 ms (1 minute), range 1000 to 600000 ms, step 1 ms.

      Multimeter

      Both

      MULTIMETER

      Polling delay:
      ms

      How often the meter values are updated (10–2000 ms). Lower values give faster response; higher values reduce CPU load.

      Show decimal point in readouts

      SIGNAL UNITS

      Display units:

      Sets the unit used for signal level readouts across all meter items. S = IARU S-scale (S1–S9+dB), dBm = -130 to 0, uV = microvolts at 50Ω.

      SIGNAL HISTORY

      History duration:
      ms

      Total time span shown in the signal history graph (1–600 000 ms).

      NEW FOR REVIEW · Every slice on the Core, from the Slice button

      Your words from the Rock: you wanted to see any slice on the Core and listen to it or take it from that menu. Here the toolbar's Slice button opens a list of every live slice on the Core, not only this pan's, and each row says who controls it and who else is listening, with Listen and Take control as real buttons. Listen on a slice on another pan jumps the band to that slice and shows its full flag, so you see what you are listening to; one button brings you back to your own band. Every refusal and notice is the Core's own words as it sends them. Every button in the phones below responds: tap it. Frequencies, device names and which slices exist are example data. Your own slices' flags on the band are today's; the flag of a slice you join is the approved finger-size flag from the next section.

      Replaced: the first proposal showed a slice you listen to on another pan only as a tag at the band's edge that opened a card. Your ruling of 30 September replaced it: Listen jumps to the slice and shows its flag. A second ruling that day: every slice is up for grabs, and the Core now allows it. Take control works on the Core's own slice too; the only time it is greyed is while the slice is transmitting, and a take from an older app goes through. A third: Take control never asks anyone, a person at the Core's desktop included. It takes the slice at once and the former holder stays on listening; the earlier frame that asked the desktop and waited for an answer is gone. And a fourth: on a listened slice's flag the owner block is one slim row, and your volume, mute and Stop listening live in the flag's own speaker panel.

      WordsDotted amber underline: the phone's own words, drawn for your call. Where neither the Core nor the desktop has words ("This pan", "Another pan", "Also listening", "Make active", "Only what this phone hears", "Listen in instead", and the flag's short owner words such as "The Core controls A"), the phone supplies them. The underline is a board marking, not part of the screen.

      NameDashed violet box: a placeholder. Shack desktop and JJ's iPad stand for whatever each device is called; the phone shows each device's own name as the Core sends it, else "a phone", "a tablet" or "a computer", and "the Core" only for a slice nobody holds or a headless Core's own. On a Core hosted by a desktop, the desktop is named by its own device name.

      The list

      One row per live slice, in letter order, never regrouped. A row never moves under your finger when you tap Listen or Take control, and the letters match the desktop's. Each row shows the letter in its colour, frequency, mode, band, whether it is on this pan, who controls it in the Core's words, and who else is listening. Your own slices are one 44 pt button each: tap to make it active, which also closes the list. Another device's slice has Listen and Take control. A slice you listen to has Stop listening, Take control and your own volume and mute; on another pan, the top of its row is also a button that jumps to its band (marked Showing while you are there). A greyed button keeps its place with the Core's reason under it.

While you only listen, the controls that would change it are greyed with the Core's words, Take control is right there, and the speaker tab stays live with your own volume, mute and Stop listening; taking control un-greys everything. The speaker tab stays live: its panel is the flag's own Audio panel, where AF Gain and MUTE are your volume and mute on this phone only, with Stop listening under them; the rest of the panel is dimmed. Take control takes the slice at once, with no question to anyone; the owner row reads Taking control… for the Core's answer, then goes, and the flag is a normal one, on the slice's own band.       NEW FOR REVIEW · Flag controls at finger size, in the desktop flag's rows

      Your call from the phone: the S-meter was cramped under the digits and the flag regrouped in large type. This redraw follows the desktop flag's rows top to bottom and keeps one layout at every text size. The flag stays 200 pt wide. Every button is at least 40 pt wide; the header and the tabs are 44 pt tall and the frequency, the number pad's target, is 40 pt tall; no two touch areas overlap. The tables below are measured on this page. Every frame uses look 2, your pick. Labels and menu items are the desktop flag's own. Every button in the phones below responds: tap it. Frequencies, antennas, device names, the RADE reading and the second radio are example data.

      WordsDotted amber underline: the phone's own words, drawn for your call. Where neither the Core nor the desktop has words for a reason (listen only, no BYPS on this radio, slice A cannot close), the phone supplies them. The underline is a board marking, not part of the screen.

      The rows, as the desktop flag has them

      1. Header, 44 pt. The antenna button (receive over transmit, BYPS beside them while it is on), the filter width, then at the right the TX badge and the slice letter. 2. The owner row, only while another device controls the slice: one 44 pt row, the height of the header, with who controls it in short words at the left and a compact Take control at the right, outlined like the flag's other buttons. 3. The frequency across the flag's full width, 40 pt tall: tap it for the number pad. 4. A 4 pt gap, the desktop's own spacer, so the scale never touches the frequency box. 5. The S-meter on its own 24 pt row: the S1 to +40 scale, the bar and the dBm readout beside it. It is not a button. 6. The RADE row, only in RADE, as the desktop's. 7. The tabs, 44 pt: 🔊, DSP, mode, X/RIT. VAX stays at the foot of the Audio panel, your earlier ruling, so the mode tab fits RADE-L.

      The step leaves the flag face. It is the X/RIT panel's bottom row, the desktop's step cycle button: it reads the step in hertz, as the desktop's does, and each tap moves to the next step, wrapping from 10000 Hz back to 1 Hz.

      One layout at every text size. Every row, button and gap is the same size and in the same place in standard and large type. Only the words grow with the phone's text size setting, up to 125 percent of standard, and then stop: at every larger setting the flag looks as it does at the cap. The tab words stop sooner, at 14 px (12 px at standard type), set a quarter point tighter at the cap, and the tabs are 40, 41.5, 67.5 and 51 pt wide, so every tab label, RADE-U included, keeps at least 6 pt from its separators and the flag's edge. The meter's numbers are drawn on the bar, so they have caps of their own: the scale at 8.5 px (the desktop's is 8 px) and the dBm readout at 11 px (the desktop's is 10 px), so the seven labels keep clear of each other and the widest reading, -127 dBm, stays beside the bar. The flag is 158 pt tall, and 176 pt in RADE with its row; the menus and panels that drop from the flag keep growing with the setting, as before, because they scroll.

      Before and after, flat at the band's scale

      Slice B in RADE-L, as you saw it: before, the flag as it was on this board; after, the redraw. Standard and large type side by side, at the same scale. Under them, the redraw in LSB, without the RADE row.

      • Antennas (the RX and TX antenna buttons and BYPS, merged): one menu with both pickers and the BYPS switch.

      Before and after on the phone

      The same band, slice B active in RADE-L, before and after, upright and turned sideways, standard and large type. Every frame is at the same scale as its neighbour.

      134 pt tall. The meter squeezed under the digits inside the frequency button.

      After

      176 pt tall in RADE, the desktop's rows. Tap TX to move transmit to slice B, the lock to lock it, the digits for the number pad. ✕ closes the slice here (the board puts it back).

      On the band

      Transmit on slice A. Upright, the slice that is not active folds as it does today (your D9): only the active flag is full.

      Antennas and More

      The antenna button shows both antennas, receive in blue over transmit in red, and BYPS in amber beside them while it is on. It opens one menu with both pickers, in the desktop's sections, and the BYPS switch with the desktop's words. On a radio without BYPS the switch stays, greyed, with its reason. More holds the desktop flag's right-click menu.

      X/RIT, with the step

      RIT and XIT, each with its arrows by the slice's step and its 0, and the step cycle button under them. Tap it: 100 Hz, 500 Hz, 1000 Hz, 10000 Hz, 1 Hz, 10 Hz.

      Disabled, never hidden: every button stays in its place. A greyed button says why when tapped.

      TX and More's Make this the TX slice are greyed. Tap TX for the reason, the phone's own words.

      One owner row under the header, where the desktop puts its access line: Shack desktop controls B and a compact Take control. The flag grows by that one row. The controls are dimmed as the take-over section draws them; a tap on one gives the Core's words, Slice B is controlled by Shack desktop. Take control to change it., and nudges the owner row. The speaker tab stays live.

      The same one row at the same height; the owner words stop at 12.5 px and Take control at the tab words' cap, 14 px, so a device name keeps to two lines beside it.

      Both flags stay full while they fit. The second flag also needs room for the buttons beside it, so it folds when the two slices' lines are closer than 246 pt (the 200 pt flag, a 2 pt gap and the 44 pt button column, at both type sizes), which is about 13.5 kHz on a 48 kHz span across the 874 pt band. The redraw keeps that rule: the flag is no wider.

      NEW FOR REVIEW · TX EQ curve on the TX Equalizer page

      Tools → TX Equalizer. The Core's parametric curve moves up the page, under Equalizer and Profile, where the old "Parametric curve" card at the bottom said to edit the curve at the Core. The curve is drawn as the Core sends it, from the curve's low end to its high end on a scale of −24 to +24 dB with the 0 dB line marked, each point numbered. Above it, one line says which EQ is on the air. Under it, a point editor and the curve's values as a list. Every change uses a visible, labelled control: − and + buttons with the step written beside them, a field that opens the number pad, the desktop's 5-band, 10-band and 18-band choice, and its Reset. The curve drawn is always the one the Core sends back, never the one the phone asked for. Nothing needs a drag, a press and hold or a hidden gesture, and nothing on this page keys the radio. Every curve, profile and device name here is example data. The first curve is the worked example from the link document. Each phone scrolls inside its page, and on the board its buttons work: choose a point, step it, change Bands, or Reset.

      A saved curve on the air

      TX EQ on, Legacy EQ off, so the curve shapes the audio. Point 3 is chosen. Example curve (the link document's worked example).

      The ten bands on the air

      Legacy EQ on: the line says the ten-band EQ is on the air. The curve still shows, marked as not in use. Example curve.

      EQ off

      TX EQ off: neither the curve nor the ten bands shape the audio. The curve still shows and can still be changed. Example curve.

      The default curve

      A factory TX profile has no saved curve. The Core sends its flat curve: ten points from 0 to 4000 Hz at 0 dB, Q 4.

      Straight lines

      With Shape set to Straight lines, lines join the points and Q is not used: its column shows "--" and its control is greyed with the reason. Example curve.

      The saved curve cannot be read

      The Core sends "unavailable". The page says so in place of a line, and never draws a flat one. The list and the editor are empty and greyed; Reset stays live and gives the profile the Core's flat curve.

      An older Core

      The Core does not send the curve. The drawing, the editor and the list are greyed, each with the reason.

      No Core connected

      As the rest of this page does today: the last values stay, dimmed, and every control is greyed with "The Core is not connected." Example curve.

      Changing the curve

      The point editor

      Previous and Next choose a point, as the list and the numbered marks on the curve do. Each value has −, + and a field. Example curve.

      The curve's values

      Shape, Bands (5, 10 or 18, as on the desktop), the curve's own preamp, the range, Reset and every point. Each row in the list chooses that point. Example curve.

      Typing a value

      A field opens the number pad the app already has, with a decimal point added for gain and Q. Example value.

      After a change

      The curve is redrawn from the Core's answer. Save sits next to the profile; nothing marks the profile as changed, as on the desktop. Example: point 3 raised from −1.5 to +2.0 dB.

      While transmitting

      A Core at transmit settings version 11 or later: every TX EQ control stays live on the air, as on the desktop, Save included, from the device the Core takes transmit settings from. A line says a change reaches the air at once. Example curve.

      While transmitting, an older Core

      Below transmit settings version 11 the Core takes no TX EQ change on the air, so every TX EQ control is greyed with its words until the radio stops. Choosing a point still works. Example curve.

      The first and last points

      They sit at the ends of the range, so their frequency is set by Low and High, as on the desktop. The control stays on screen, greyed with the reason. Example curve.

      Changed on another device

      The page redraws from the Core's curve at once and says so. The chosen point stays chosen by its number. Example curve.

      A curve of another point count

      An old profile can hold a curve of another count, here 7 points. It shows as it is, and none of 5-band, 10-band or 18-band is chosen. Example curve.

      The Core refuses a change

      Changing a point of that 7-point curve: the Core's own words show under the editor, the curve stays as the Core has it, and Bands is the way out. Example curve.

      A Core that cannot take changes

      The Core sends the curve but cannot change it from the phone. The curve draws in full; every curve control, Reset included, is greyed with the Core's reason.

      Another device has the transmitter

      The transmit settings' own rule: every TX EQ control and Save are greyed with the Core's words. The device name is an example.

      Large type

      At a large text size the curve keeps its width, and each value's name sits on its own line above its controls. Example curve.

      Large type, the list

      Each point's frequency, gain and Q go on a second line under its number. Nothing is cut short. Example curve.

      Turned sideways

      The curve stays on the left and the rest of the page scrolls on the right, so the curve is in view while a point changes. Example curve.

      Sideways, large type

      Both sides scroll; every name and value stays whole. Example curve.

      What the desktop's editor has, and where it is here

      The desktop's parametric panel in its TX EQ dialog, control by control.

      NEW FOR REVIEW · Transmit stage meters

      The desktop's seven transmit stage readings as one strip in the TX panel, directly under Mic level and above PROC, VOX and MON. In AM, SAM or DSB the AM Mod Monitor still comes last, below PROC, VOX and MON. Each bar carries its name, its scale in dB (the desktop bar's own range) and its reading; a thin white mark shows the recent peak, which the phone keeps from the readings it gets, like the desktop's peak marker and the phone's own Mic level. The strip only shows readings: nothing in it can be tapped, held or dragged. Every reading here is example data, not a live measurement. Each phone scrolls inside its TX panel.

      Keyed in USB

      Example readings in all seven. While the radio transmits the Core sends them ten times a second.

      Not transmitting

      Off the air the Core sends a reading only when it changes, so the strip keeps the last ones it sent, dimmed, with a line saying so. Example readings.

      No transmit readings on the Core

      When the Core has nothing to measure (it sends "no reading"), every value shows "--" and the bars stay empty. Never a 0.

      An older Core

      The Core does not send these readings. The seven bars are greyed and the reason is said once, above them.

      Keyed in AM: where the strip sits

      Mic level, then the strip, then PROC, VOX and MON, then the AM Mod Monitor as approved. Example readings.

      Large type

      At a large text size each name and reading sit on one line with the bar under them, full width. Nothing is cut short. Example readings.

      The seven readings

      Names and scales as the desktop's bars show them, in the order the sound passes through the transmitter.

      Turned sideways, keyed in USB

      The TX panel slides in from the right, clear of the camera; the strip is the same, under Mic level. Example readings.

      Sideways, large type

      The panel scrolls further; every name and reading stays whole. Example readings.

      iPad applet column, keyed in USB

      The TX applet in the column on the right carries the same strip under Mic level; the column scrolls to it. Example readings.

      NEW FOR REVIEW · AM Mod Monitor

      The desktop's AM Mod Monitor on the phone's TX panel. It appears while the transmitting slice is in AM, SAM or DSB, below the panel's usual controls, and shows the Core's readings: positive and negative peaks with their holds, asymmetry, the carrier level and lamp, the peak flashers and the envelope scope. Every reading and frequency here is labelled example data, not a live measurement. Tap RESET, the source buttons, Settings, and the steppers inside the sheet; each phone scrolls inside its TX panel.

      Keyed in AM, carrier OK

      Example readings. TX I/Q is the source. PA feedback is greyed with its reason because PureSignal is off on the Core's radio.

      Carrier low, both flashers latched

      Example readings with PureSignal running, so PA feedback can be picked. The flashers stay lit until RESET.

      In AM, not transmitting

      No carrier: bars empty, every reading "--", the lamp off. The monitor waits for the radio to transmit.

      Meter style: Meters

      The desktop's second style: a lit analog pair with the asymmetry bar between them, and the green scope. Picked in Settings; this phone only.

      Settings, from the monitor

      The Settings button opens this sheet: source, flasher thresholds and meter style for this phone, and the Core's feedback receiver, marked as shared.

      An older Core

      The Core does not send the monitor. Everything is greyed, with the reason above it.

      Not connected

      The link is down. The monitor is greyed with its own reason until the Core is back.

      In USB: no monitor

      For contrast. The transmitting slice is in USB, which is not AM, SAM or DSB, so the TX panel ends after PROC, VOX and MON.

      Large type

      The same monitor at a large text size: readings stack one per row and the buttons grow. Example readings.

      Lamps and flashers

      What each lamp means, as the desktop shows it. The lamp takes the first that applies, in this order.

      NO CARRIERNot transmitting in AM, SAM or DSB, or no carrier. Readings show "--".
      CARRIER HIGHCarrier above 98% of full scale.
      CARRIER LOWCarrier below 5% of full scale.
      CARRIER OKCarrier present and in range.
      +PEAKLights when a positive peak reaches its threshold (desktop default 125%) and stays lit until RESET.
      -PEAKLights when a negative peak reaches its threshold (desktop default 95%) and stays lit until RESET.

      RESET clears the Core's peaks and flashers for every device watching the monitor, as on the desktop.

      Turned sideways, keyed in AM

      The TX panel slides in from the right, clear of the camera; the monitor is the same, below the panel's controls. Example readings.

      Sideways, large type

      At a large text size the panel scrolls further; nothing is cut off or hidden. Example readings.

      Pairing and connecting: the states in between

      New this round, for your approval, before the listening build is built. The Core's own words appear as it sends them.

      Pair with a code, after an address

      The Core it pairs with, where to find the code, and this phone's name as the Core will list it (D65: "iPhone" until Apple grants the phone's own name).

      A wrong code

      The Core's words, and its wait before the new code (5, 10, 20, then 40 seconds).

      Pairing closed

      After the fifth wrong code in a row the Core closes pairing, and only the Core can open it again.

      Your Cores: every case

      A Core that removed or forgot this phone stays in the list with Pair. On this network: Pair is one tap; Use code opens the code with the address filled in (new: a Core already paired with others that opened pairing for one more device lists this way); a closed one says so.

      Local network not allowed

      iOS asked and the answer was no, so this Wi-Fi couldn't be tried. The phone says where to allow it.

      The phone's key can't be read

      New: after an erase and restore the phone may no longer read the key it signs in with. It says so, makes a new key when asked, and every Core then needs pairing again.

      When things aren't right

      Each screen names its own cause, so you know whether to walk to the radio, the station computer or your phone. Your call on versions: every app release still talks to a station one version behind, so an App Store update never locks you out; only a station two versions behind is refused.

      The radio is off

      The station answers but can't hear the radio. The desktop's DISCONNECTED over the band, with the last frame and the five-second retry.

      The Core isn't answering

      The station computer is off, asleep or offline. The phone says what it tried and what to check.

      The Core needs updating

      Only when the station is two versions behind this app. The phone names both versions instead of failing without a reason.

      An older Core

      One version behind, or less: the phone connects and greys only what the station can't do yet.

      This phone is offline

      Not the station's fault. The phone waits for a network, and says the Core has already unkeyed.

      Spot Hub on the phone

      The desktop's Spot Hub is a ten-tab dialog. On the phone it's a Tools page: the spot list and the display first, then each source with its status, then your identity. Each part is tagged by where it lives: the sources and the list at the station, the look on the band on this phone.

      Spot Hub

      Your call: one page instead of ten tabs. Each source shows whether it's running and taps through to its own page.

      Spot List

      The station's spots, newest first, with the desktop's source pills and a band filter. Tap one to tune.

      Display

      The desktop's knobs with its defaults. Lifetime and clearing belong to the station, so they're marked that way.

      A source: Cluster

      The connection, the live console and a command line, as on the desktop's Cluster tab.

      Spots on the band

      The desktop's spot overlay, carried over as it is. Callsigns start halfway down the spectrum, stack down three levels and overflow into amber +N badges, coloured by DXCC: red a new country, orange a new band, gold a new mode, grey worked before. The spots come from the station, which runs the cluster, POTA and other spot clients; how they look is set on each phone. On the phone they never start behind a flag.

      On the band

      Tap a callsign to tune to it. The flags stay on top; the spots sit in the lower half, as on the desktop.

      Tap +N

      The spots a badge hides, as a list. Tap one to tune.

      Press and hold a spot

      What the desktop shows when you hover: mode, source, spotter, comment and time.

      Sideways

      Your call: spots start under the lowest flag and use only the rows that fit, with the rest in +N badges. Upright, that's still halfway down, as on the desktop.

      First launch

      What someone sees the first time they open the app from the App Store, before they have a station. It follows the pairing design: a new station waits for its first device, one tap claims it on the same Wi-Fi, and its code works from anywhere.

      Welcome

      What the app needs, in one picture, and the two ways on. Your call: a station is required, with no demo mode.

      Looking on this Wi-Fi

      iOS asks once before an app can search the local network. The line under the question is the app's own.

      Found it

      Nothing paired yet, and the new station on this Wi-Fi, ready to claim with one tap. From elsewhere, its code works.

      Paired

      The microphone is asked for now, so iOS never interrupts the first transmission. Listening works without it.

      Set up a Core

      What a station is, the two ways to run one, and what it does on its own.

      Tuning dial

      Your calls: all three, picked in Setup on this phone, on the page the desktop calls Navigation, and off until someone picks one. Each detent moves the active slice one step, with a haptic tick and a firmer bump on each whole kilohertz. The steps are Thetis's full list. Drag around a knob to try it. A browser can't make the ticks, so the mark at the top flashes instead.

      Knob on the waterfall

      Opposite PTT, so one thumb keys and the other tunes. Tap the middle to change the step.

      Changing the step

      From 1 Hz to 10 MHz. Each slice keeps its own step on each band, as on the desktop.

      Knob in a sheet

      Tap the frequency to raise a big knob, with the steps in a row above it. More room to turn, but it covers the waterfall and PTT while it's up.

      Thumbwheel

      A flat wheel along the bottom of the waterfall, rolled with one thumb like the camera's zoom. The step sits at its left end.

      Choosing a dial

      Setup, General, Navigation, as on the desktop. A new install starts at Off; here someone has picked the knob.

      Sideways

      The knob on the sideways layout: PTT under the left thumb, the knob under the right.

      iPhone turned sideways

      Turned sideways, iOS hides the status bar and keeps controls clear of the camera and the rounded corners. The band itself runs edge to edge, like a photo.

      Same layout, turned

      Your call: everything where it was upright, with the station in the middle of the toolbar. The wider band keeps both flags full.

      Keyed

      The toggle PTT latched, with RF power, SWR and your mic level on the waterfall beside it.

      TX panel

      The panels slide in from the sides, clear of the camera, with the amp and tuner as upright.

      Charging on its side

      Locked on a charger, iOS shows the lock-screen card at twice the size, edge to edge. It only reports, as you decided.

      Lock screen

      Two iOS rules shape this: an app can't turn the microphone on while the phone is locked, and buttons on the lock screen wait for Face ID. Your calls: locking the phone unkeys, so a locked phone never transmits from its screen and the card only reports; the one exception is a hardware PTT button, through Apple's Push to Talk.

      Listening

      The station, the slice and the signal. iOS limits how often the card can change, so the reading steps every few seconds.

      Locked while keyed

      Your call: locking the phone stops transmitting. The screen stays awake while you're keyed, so it only locks when you lock it.

      Link lost

      The phone lights up and buzzes, then keeps retrying until you cancel.

      Back on the air

      Reconnected by relay, with transmit off.

      In another app

      The same card lives in the Dynamic Island while another app is in front. The phone is unlocked here, so its buttons work in one tap. On iPhones without the island, the card shows only on the lock screen, and a lost link arrives as a banner.

      Listening

      The slice and the frequency stay in view beside the camera.

      Switch apps while keyed

      Your call: you stay on the air. TX and the clock stay in red at the top of every app, with the orange microphone dot.

      Press and hold the island

      It opens to the card. UNKEY works in one tap here.

      Link lost while keyed

      The island opens by itself and the phone buzzes. The station has already unkeyed.

      On the band

      Receiving

      Your layout with NereusSDR's flags. Slice B folds when it would land on A.

      Keyed

      The toggle PTT latched: timer, the orange TX filter, the MOX-gated passband, and RF power, SWR and your mic level on the waterfall. Your call: the mic level is here as well as in the TX panel.

      RX panel

      The quick receive subset, one tap from the toolbar.

      TX panel, with amp and tuner

      RF power, TUNE and MOX, with the Power Genius OPERATE toggle and the Tuner Genius TUNE.

      Tabs

      Modes

      The full set for the active slice, now with the front end: preamp, step attenuator and antennas.

      Tools

      The desktop's fourteen tools in its order, marked by where each one runs.

      Radio

      The station and link, the radio at a glance, the accessories and the Radio menu.

      Setup

      The desktop's Setup tree, marked Station, This phone or Both.

      Devices

      Paired devices, one-tap revoke, Add a device and the key backup prompt.

      Connecting

      Your Cores

      Paired stations, then any unclaimed ones on this network.

      Pair with a code

      A number and two words, typed once.

      Enter an address

      The address alone, IPv6 without brackets, and the port in a field of its own.

      Link lost while keyed

      The station unkeys itself; the phone keeps retrying and lets you stop.

      Back on the air

      Reconnected by relay, with transmit left off.

      Amps and tuner

      Power Genius XL

      Gauges, OPERATE, the TX interlock, fault history and Advanced.

      Tuner Genius XL

      Relays, TUNE, the OPERATE cycle, labelled antennas and tune memory.

      RF-Kit RF2K-S

      OPERATE, gauges, volts and amps, antennas; tuner buttons wait on firmware.

      Interlock says no

      Amp in STANDBY with the interlock on Block: PTT explains itself.

      iPad

      The applet column

      Band on the left; the analog S-meter, RX and TX (with the amp and tuner) on the right. Both slices keep full flags where they fit.
